title: Carriers strike Rabaul

facts.text: After U.S. Marines landed at Empress Augusta Bay on Bougainville on 1 November 1943, Japan sent Vice Adm. Takeo Kurita's heavy cruisers from Truk to Rabaul to attack the beachhead.

Admiral William F. Halsey had no surface force able to stop the cruisers, so he ordered the carriers Saratoga and Princeton under Rear Adm. Frederick C. Sherman to strike the ships at Rabaul, one of the best defended harbors in the Pacific.
Halsey later wrote: "This was the most desperate emergency that confronted me in my entire term as COMSOPAC."
Halsey wrote that he expected both air groups to be cut to pieces and both carriers to be badly hit, if not lost, and that he tried not to remember that his son Bill was aboard one of them.
On the morning of 5 November 1943, Sherman launched all 97 of his planes: 52 Hellcat fighters, 23 Avenger torpedo bombers and 22 Dauntless dive bombers.
With every carrier fighter in the strike, Navy fighters flying from Barakoma on Vella Lavella covered the carriers instead.
The planes caught the Japanese cruisers refueling in Simpson Harbor and damaged six cruisers, four of them heavily: Atago, Maya, Takao and Mogami. Chikuma was also damaged.
A bomb hit Maya above an engine room and started a major fire that killed 70 men. Two bombs holed Takao below the waterline and killed 23.
Near misses killed 22 men aboard Atago, including her captain, and a bomb set Mogami afire and killed 19.

Aboard one Saratoga Avenger, gunner Kenneth Bratton put a tourniquet on his own shattered knee and stayed conscious until he was lifted from his turret. Navy photographer Paul T. Barnett, in the same plane, was killed while photographing an approaching Zero head on.
American plane losses were light for so risky a raid, though counts differ by source.
By the next morning only one cruiser and a few destroyers were left at Rabaul. The damaged cruisers went back to Truk, and the cruiser threat to the Bougainville beachhead was over.

On 11 November Halsey struck again, adding Rear Adm. Alfred E. Montgomery's carriers Essex, Bunker Hill and Independence. The raid sank the destroyer Suzunami, and a Japanese air counterattack lost heavily without damaging Montgomery's carriers.

film.shot_notes: No film of the 5 November strike was found on the NARA catalog. 428-NPC-1810 (NARA 76211) is the Japanese air attack on the carriers during the 11 November follow up raid, a different event six days later, so it is not used. Story Card from photos.
